title: Boys is a Four Letter Word
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles argues that the so-called problem with boys is partly one that schools manufacture, because teacher reward systems favour the habits typically associated with girls and criticise those typically associated with boys. He asks teachers to audit who is actually praised in each year group, and claims the resulting photographs would show smiling faces almost entirely girls. He rejects the retreat to social explanations such as absent fathers or screens, on the ground that a school that cannot make a difference has no point, and says expectations matter more than boy-friendly techniques. He then defends praise (properly aimed at effort, following Dweck) as a way to break the negative cycle for the bottom ten students in a class. The second half is a practical toolkit, taken from his book The Slightly Awesome Teacher, of competitions, merit fractions, note-taking games, public marks and quiet signals that reward process and build consistency. The archive value is the audit of teacher bias and the move from praise principles to concrete behaviour routines.
points: Teacher reports show a large bias toward praising girls and criticising boys even where attainment is similar, so schools may stereotype boys within weeks of arrival.
Salles dismisses social explanations as an excuse: if school cannot make a difference, teachers have no purpose, and teacher expectations matter more than boy-friendly tricks.
Dweck-style praise is not wrong; it should target directed effort, and students who are mostly criticised need a deliberate way to be praised meaningfully.
Small competitions, merit fractions and public recognition reward the process of work and reduce marking while improving behaviour.
Rewarding personal bests rather than raw outcomes guards against the bias that automatically favours girls effort.
quotes: Compare these to their KS2 results, and you will see the problem straight away: the boys have just arrived, and we have already stereotyped them, we have already told them that they are not good enough.
The results were fascinating: they showed a huge bias towards praising girls and criticizing boys, even where attainment was similar.

Thanks to the work of Carol Dweck on growth mindset, many teachers assume that praise is wrong. It isn’t. Dweck’s work asks us to be careful to praise directed effort and perseverance, not intelligence or ability.
Add up the times that they are criticised, and compare them to the number of times they are praised. The ratio is huge; it feels entirely negative.

Another huge advantage of this is that it reminds you never to talk while your students are still talking. This is a fundamental skill which teachers frequently forget, because they want to move on. It is the easiest way to lose a class, though.

Behaviour is improved if students are aware of their own growing success. For example, give students several facts/ideas/spellings to learn. Get them to visualise it, tell them you will not be testing them by asking them questions, but by getting them to reproduce the whole lot.

Students are likely to perform better if they are intrinsically motivated, rather than extrinsically. To encourage this, you might wish to reward effort, rather than outcome. There is a danger that this will automatically favour girls, however, because of our biased perception of their effort.
